Dexter King, left, Bernice King and Martin Luther King III attend a 2006 tribute for their late mother. "I'm disappointed that our personal family disagreement, as it relates to the family business, has evolved into being handled in a public legal forum," he said. "It is my hope that this inappropriate and false claim by my siblings will be swiftly resolved and we can go about the business of focusing on our parents' tremendous legacy." The Rev. King's wife, Coretta Scott King, also devoted her life to the civil rights movement, died in 2006. Attorneys for Bernice King and Martin Luther King III would not say Friday how much money they are accusing Dexter King of taking from their mother's estate. Bernice King is the administrator of that estate. Dexter King, the suit says, controls their father's estate, which is registered as a Georgia corporation. All three children are shareholders in that corporation. The lawsuit names Dexter King and the corporation as defendants. It alleges that last month, the defendants "converted substantial funds from the estate's financial account at Bank of America for their own use." Harmon Caldwell, an Atlanta attorney representing the plaintiffs, said Dexter King is a signatory on the account, but "was not authorized to transfer the funds," and gave his sister "no notice that those funds were being transferred." The suit says that as a result of the transfer, "plaintiffs have and will suffer financial loss." The lawsuit lists Bernice King as a plaintiff both individually and as administrator of their mother's estate. Separately, the suit says Dexter King "has wrongfully appropriated assets belonging to the [estate of the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.] or its shareholders for his own benefit." Caldwell said Dexter King has refused to say what has happened with some of the corporation's money. "I can't tell you that he's gone out and used corporate assets for his own living expenses," the attorney said. "What I can tell you for certainty is that by not providing Martin and Bernice with information about how the corporation is using its assets, he is essentially using those assets, appropriating those assets for his own benefit." The plaintiffs' attorneys would not estimate the size of either estate. But one, Jock Smith, noted that a collection of King's manuscripts and other items was sold in 2006 for a reported $32 million. "I don't think it was a substantial corporation of any sort before that," Smith said. Over the years, the family of the civil rights leader has zealously protected its financial interests, at times taking legal steps even against the media for showing some of King's most famous speeches. In 2005, some news agencies reported on the King Center, a nonprofit, having put millions of dollars into a for-profit business run by Dexter King. The family rejected allegations of wrongdoing, and has generally pushed to keep financial matters private. Smith said his clients made repeated efforts to reach out to their brother in recent weeks before deciding to take legal action. Smith agreed with the suggestion that it was emotionally tough for the King children to file the suit. "That would be the understatement of the year, Smith said.

**ATLANTA (CNN)** — Decades after Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. preached a vision of unity and brotherhood to the world, his surviving children are once again locked in a bitter, high-stakes legal war among themselves over the civil rights icon’s historic legacy and personal property.

In the latest chapter of a painful and deeply public family feud, Bernice King and Martin Luther King III have filed a lawsuit against their brother, Dexter King, accusing him of mismanaging their parents’ estate and attempting to sell off some of their father's most cherished historical items.

At the heart of the latest court filing in Fulton County Superior Court is a stark disagreement over two prized artifacts: Dr. King’s 1964 Nobel Peace Prize medal and his personal traveling Bible—the same Bible used by President Barack Obama during his second inauguration in 2013.

According to court documents, Dexter King, acting as the president and CEO of Estate of Martin Luther King Jr. Inc., voted alongside a court-appointed custodian to sell the two physical items to a private buyer. Bernice King, an ordained minister and the CEO of the King Center in Atlanta, vehemently opposed the sale, describing the items as "sacred."

"Our father’s legacy is not for sale," Bernice King said at a press conference outside the historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta. "These items are precious heirlooms, not only to our family, but to the world. Selling them strips away the spiritual dignity of what our parents fought and died for."

### A corporation vs. a cause

The lawsuit exposes a fundamental rift that has plagued the King family for years: whether Dr. King's legacy should be managed as a sacred public trust or as a tightly guarded commercial corporation.

The Estate of Martin Luther King Jr. Inc. operates as a private company controlled by the siblings, holding the copyrights to Dr. King's speeches, writings, and image. Under Georgia law, decisions regarding estate assets require a majority vote among the shareholders—the three surviving siblings. 

Dexter King, who has long overseen the estate’s corporate affairs from Los Angeles, has maintained that his actions are aimed at securing the financial stability of the family estate and protecting the intellectual property of their father. Lawyers for the estate argue that Dexter is fulfilling his legal fiduciary duty.

In court filings, attorneys representing the estate argued that selling the items was necessary to generate funds for the estate's ongoing operation and legal fees. 

"The estate has a legal obligation to manage its assets responsibly," a spokesman for the estate said in a statement. "This is a business matter that should be handled through proper corporate channels, not aired out in the media."

### A history of family courtroom battles

This is far from the first time the King siblings have resorted to legal action to resolve personal and financial disputes.

*   **In 2008**, Bernice King and Martin Luther King III sued Dexter King, accusing him of mismanaging estate funds and diverting money from the estate to his private venture, King Inc.
*   **That same year**, Dexter King countersued, alleging that Bernice was improperly using the King Center’s assets and withholding key records related to their mother, Coretta Scott King, who died in 2006.
*   **In 2013**, the estate sued the King Center—led by Bernice—demanding the return of Dr. King’s personal papers and revoking the center's license to use Dr. King’s image and name.

The recurring litigation has drawn quiet dismay from veterans of the Civil Rights Movement who marched alongside Dr. King in the 1960s.

"It breaks your heart," said Andrew Young, a former U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations and close confidant of Dr. King, speaking to CNN. "Martin gave everything he had to the world. To see his children fighting over his memory in a courtroom is painful for anyone who loved him."

### What comes next

A judge in Fulton County is expected to hear arguments in the coming weeks on whether to block the sale of the Nobel Peace Prize medal and the Bible while the broader lawsuit proceeds. 

Legal experts say the case could ultimately force a court-ordered restructuring of how the estate is managed, or potentially lead to a court-appointed receiver taking control of the civil rights leader's physical property.

For now, the items remain locked in a secure deposit box—their ultimate fate, much like the unity of the King family, hanging in the balance of a legal system Dr. King so famously sought to transform.

The feud reached a boiling point in 2014 when Dexter and Martin III voted 2-1 to sell two of their father's most cherished possessions: his 1964 Nobel Peace Prize medal and the traveling Bible he used during the Civil Rights Movement—the same Bible used by President Barack Obama during his second inauguration.

Bernice fiercely resisted the sale, calling the items "sacred" and refusing to surrender them from the King Center vault. 

"Refusing to sell our father's most cherished personal possessions is not about disrespecting my brothers," Bernice said in a statement at the time. "It is about preserving the spiritual and historical integrity of a man who gave his life for humanity."

The legal battle forced former President Jimmy Carter to step in as a mediator in 2015 to help the siblings reach a confidential settlement.

### **Commercialization vs. Preservation**

The estate's aggressive management strategy has drawn sharp criticism from historians and civil rights veterans, who argue that restricting access to King’s speeches hinders public education. 

"The tragedy is that the financial battles have sometimes overshadowed the movement itself," said David Garrow, a Pulitzer Prize-winning biographer of Dr. King. "When schoolteachers or scholars have to fear copyright infringement for sharing the 'I Have a Dream' speech, the estate's priorities have drifted far from the founder's mission."

Supporters of the estate, however, argue that protective management is necessary to prevent corporate exploitation. Over the years, the estate has turned down hundreds of commercial requests—including alcohol and commercial product endorsements—that would demean King's image. Revenue generated from legitimate licensing deals, the estate argues, funds the preservation of historical materials and supports family operations.

### **The Future of the Estate**

The dynamic of the estate shifted significantly in January 2024 following the death of Dexter Scott King after a battle with prostate cancer. 

With Dexter's passing, Martin Luther King III and Bernice King remain the sole surviving children and decision-makers of the estate. While the siblings have expressed a desire for unity in recent years, the future handling of Dr. King’s intellectual property remains a delicate balancing act.

As the nation continues to draw upon Dr. King's words during times of social tension, the family faces the ongoing challenge of protecting a commercial asset while honoring the sacred legacy of a global moral leader.
